name: AppLayout
label: App layout
description: Full-page template pairing the collapsible App sidebar with a content area, in flush, floating or inset mode, contained or full width.

props.name: activeTertiaryKey
props.description: Active third-level item key, listed in the sidebar's side panel

props.name: subNav
props.description:
Where sub-items show: straight into the sidebar's side panel, or its
accordion (see AppSidebar).

props.name: children
props.description: Page content — centred in the main area

props.name: toolbar
props.description:
A bar at the top of the content column, held there while the page
scrolls: a search trigger, a few icon buttons, the account's avatar.
It runs the width the content runs (`width`), on the content's own
surface, in every `layout`. Lay its items out yourself, for example
with a Toolbar or a flex row; the slot only seats and pins them.

props.name: layout
props.description:
How the rail and the content meet the page, one of the three app shell
modes. `flush` runs the rail edge to edge on the shell
colour behind a hairline, the content centred beside it on the crisp
app surface, nothing raised. `floating` floats the rail as a glass card,
the content still centred. `inset` runs the rail flush on the shell
colour and sets the content in a raised surface (hairline and floating
shadow) inset from the other edges, which scrolls inside itself, and is
the default. How wide the content runs is `width`, apart from the mode.

props.name: width
props.description:
How wide the content runs, in any `layout`: `contained` centres it at
the contained width (1120px here, or `--ds-shell-contained-width` set
on the layout); `full` runs it the whole width the mode leaves it. An
app's working column, so it takes none of SiteLayout's site-scale
`containedWidth` steps. `inset` no longer forces full width, as it did
up to 1.32: pass `width="full"` for that edge-to-edge inset.

props.name: theme
props.description:
Colour scheme: 'dark' pins the layout to the dark theme (the historical
behaviour and the default); 'inherit' drops the pin so the layout
follows the surrounding data-theme like any other component.

props.name: linkComponent
props.description:
The component its links render with, such as Next.js's `Link`, so they
navigate through the app's router; passed on to the AppSidebar rail. Wins over a
LinkProvider's; a plain `<a>` when neither is set.

props.name: sidebarProps
props.description:
The rest of the AppSidebar rail's options, passed through as they are,
so an app on AppLayout has the same rail as the templates and a chat:
folding sections (`collapsibleSections`), a footer action, the top and
footer slots, the profile's more button, the drawer's entries and
labels. The props AppLayout sets itself (the sections, the profile, the
active keys, `subNav`, the logo, `layout`, the expanded state, the link
component and the rail's seat) are its own.

props.name: className
props.description: Additional CSS classes on outer wrapper

AppLayoutSidebarProps.description: The AppSidebar options AppLayout passes through untouched (`sidebarProps`).

AppSidebarLayout.description: The three app shell modes, how the rail meets the page: edge to edge behind a hairline, floating as a card, or flush beside a raised inset surface.

LinkComponent.description: A component that renders a link in place of a plain `<a>`, such as a router's.

LinkComponentProps.description:
The props a link component receives: every anchor attribute, the ref, and
an `href` that is always a string. Next.js's `Link` takes these as they
are; a router whose link takes `to` instead needs a one-line adapter:
`({ href, ...props }) => <RouterLink to={href} {...props} />`.

keys.note: The rail is AppSidebar, which carries the layout’s keys. The layout adds none of its own.

alternatives.name: SiteLayout
alternatives.when: the page is a site of pages under a top header, such as documentation
